title: Stop Doing What Works. Start Doing What Helps.
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: This article builds on Father Greg Boyle's maxim—not everything that works helps, but everything that helps, works—to challenge a pervasive pattern in modern childhood management where adults consistently choose short-term compliance over long-term formation. Using vivid examples from school hallways, restaurants, and cafeterias, the author shows how devices, silent routines, and hyper-structured environments produce outward order while quietly preventing children from developing the capacities they will need: patience, social fluency, resilience, creativity, independence, and physical confidence. The author's Architecture of Childhood framework identifies nine developmental domains—including self-regulation, social connection, agency, and purpose—and argues these grow only through repeated practice in real conditions, not through managed, frictionless environments. A powerful real-world example: when a middle school replaced silent hallways and controlled lunches with playground time and unstructured peer interaction, attendance improved, discipline fell, academic performance rose, and the school became one of only two Title I middle schools in South Carolina to earn an Excellent rating. The essay ends with a clarifying distinction: a well-managed child and a well-formed child are not the same child.
points: The works versus helps distinction is the central challenge of modern childhood: interventions that produce immediate outward compliance often erode the developmental capacities children most need to build.

The nine domains of the Architecture of Childhood—including self-regulation, resilience, independence, creativity, and purpose—grow only through repeated practice in real, mildly challenging conditions; managing away those challenges manages away the development.

When one middle school replaced silent hallways with playground time before school, children became visibly more ready to learn, discipline improved, attendance rose, and the school earned an Excellent rating—proving that what truly helps also works better.

A child becomes patient by repeatedly practicing waiting, socially capable by repeatedly navigating other children, and resilient by facing mild frustration without immediate rescue—these are outcomes of conditions, not curriculum.

The deepest error of modern adult decision-making around children is choosing efficiency over formation—producing outward order while causing inward erosion, then being confused when children seem less patient, less resilient, and less self-directed.
quotes: Not everything that works helps, but everything that helps, works.
It solved the adult’s problem. It may have weakened the child.
Children are not meant to be successfully stored like luggage until instruction begins. They are social creatures. Physical creatures. Meaning-making creatures.

A well-managed child and a well-formed child are not necessarily the same child. That may be one of the great mistakes of modern adulthood. We have become so skilled at producing outward order that we sometimes fail to notice inward erosion.
We keep choosing efficiency over formation. We keep choosing control over growth. We keep choosing what calms the moment over what builds the person.
What works makes adulthood easier right now. What helps builds the child who will one day be able to live without us.
